title: the abduction
hook: carried into the sky, Sita turns the whole forest into witnesses

segments.voice: Yesterday: the abduction began. A holy man at the door, a seat and water, and then a name: Ravana. Sita called him a jackal to his face. What did you say no to yesterday, and how did it feel? Day five hundred seventy-three.

Words didn't stop him. Valmiki says Ravana's face changes and his eyes go red, and the holy man's body falls away like a costume. In its place stands the king of Lanka, huge and dark as a storm cloud. He seizes Sita, and his chariot, waiting out of sight, rises into the sky. Below, the hut gets smaller and smaller. And then Sita does something unexpected. She starts talking to the forest.
screen: `THE COSTUME FALLS AWAY.` → `A CHARIOT RISES.` → `SHE TALKS TO THE FOREST.`

segments.voice: Listen to who she calls. She cries out for Rama, of course, and for Lakshmana, the brother she drove away with cruel words. Valmiki doesn't stop to settle that; he lets it hang. Then she turns to everything around her. She calls to the flowering trees of Janasthana and asks them to tell Rama. She calls to the Godavari river. She calls to the spirits of the forest, to the deer, to the birds, to anything alive that will still be there when Rama comes back. Tell him Ravana has taken Sita. That's the first idea. It sounds like panic, and partly it is. But look again, and it's also a plan. Sita knows Rama will come back to an empty hut, with nobody human there to explain. So she makes the whole forest her witnesses. Second, notice the name. She doesn't just say a demon took me. She says Ravana. She makes sure the message carries who, not only what. Third, the picture. Later in the flight, Valmiki pulls the view wide: the river, the trees, the animals running beneath the shadow of the chariot, and Sita in yellow silk against Ravana's dark shape, like lightning against a cloud. This isn't only a household's disaster. The poem wants the whole world to see it. But first, in a tall tree, Sita sees a bird she knows. An old vulture, half asleep in the branches. She calls his name.
screen: `SHE CALLS RAMA, AND LAKSHMANA.` · `THE TREES, THE RIVER, THE DEER.` · `A NAME IN THE MESSAGE: RAVANA.` · `LIGHTNING AGAINST A CLOUD.`

segments.voice: Look around wherever you are and pick three things that have been there all day: a tree outside, a wall, a cup. Let them be your witnesses for two minutes. Breathe slowly. Nothing to report, nothing to fix. Just notice that you are not unseen; the world around you has been present the whole time. When your mind runs off, come back to the three things. The bell holds the time.
The abduction. Ravana drops the disguise, and Sita, carried into the sky, turns the forest into witnesses.
Your line: the abduction. Today, if something goes wrong, tell someone right away and tell them clearly, the way Sita told the river. Day five hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Ramlila performances stage the abduction, and tellings that follow Valmiki keep Sita's cries to the forest and its creatures.

pairs: a river she asks to tell Rama
yellow silk on a dark shape
the bird she sees in a tree

myth: Sita only cries for help without a plan
she makes the forest her witnesses, so someone can tell Rama.
she names Ravana in her cries
the message carries who took her, not only what happened.
Ravana keeps his holy-man disguise as he flies
the costume falls away and he takes his own huge form.

fork.setup: you're Sita, carried into the sky. nobody human is below. what do you do?
options: stay silent and save your strength.
call to the trees, the river and the animals to tell Rama.
plead with Ravana to turn back.
fork.reveal: she calls on the whole forest, by name, to carry the message: Ravana has taken Sita.

original.note: Sanskrit sītāharaṇa: the carrying-off of Sita. a common name for this episode in tellings and plays.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sita just screams for help.
what it means: she turns the forest into witnesses and names her abductor.
what a scholar hears: Aranya 49 has Sita address the trees of Janasthana, the Godavari and the forest beings; the lightning-and-cloud image recurs in the chariot scenes.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda 49 (Ravana takes his own form; Sita calls to the forest)
Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda 52 (Sita in the sky, like lightning against a cloud)

notes: Sarga numbers follow the common (vulgate) numbering and differ between editions; confirm against the edition the Keeper uses.
Ravana's change of form (red eyes, huge size) paraphrased; Valmiki's description of heads and arms here varies by edition, so the script says only 'huge and dark'.
The lightning-against-a-cloud image and Sita's yellow silk: confirm sarga (49 or 52).
'Ramlila performances often stage...' in howItsDone is a general description; a Keeper may wish to adjust.

Editor review: fixed the order of events (the lightning-and-cloud flight image is Aranya 52, after Jatayu, so it is now marked 'later'), removed 'an hour ago' and 'surprises first-time readers', and replaced the unsourced 'audiences know her cries by heart' in howItsDone.
